questions.stem: Which structural feature causes restricted rotation in an alkene?

options.text: The pi component of the double bond
options.explanation: Tearing the sideways overlap is the only way to twist, so rotation is barred.

options.text: The sigma component of the double bond
options.explanation: Sigma bonds alone allow free rotation, as in alkanes.
Hydrogens are passengers, not the lock.

options.text: The length of the carbon chain
options.explanation: Chain length does not affect rotation about the double bond.

questions.stem: What condition must each double-bonded carbon satisfy for geometric isomerism?

options.text: It must carry a hydrogen atom
options.explanation: Hydrogen is common but not required - E / Z works without it.

options.text: It must carry two different groups
options.explanation: Only then are same-side and opposite-side arrangements distinguishable.

options.text: It must carry two identical groups
options.explanation: Identical groups make one arrangement, so no pair of isomers exists.
A double-bonded carbon holds only two substituent positions.

questions.stem: In which arrangement do the identical groups sit facing each other across the double bond?

options.explanation: That is a conformational term for single bonds, not alkene geometry.
Not a stereochemical term in this course.
Trans means across - the matching groups sit on opposing sides.
Cis means parked together on one side.

questions.stem: But-2-ene and but-1-ene: which one shows geometric isomerism?

options.explanation: The first carbon of but-1-ene carries two hydrogens, so no pair of arrangements exists.
But-1-ene fails the two-different-groups test on its first carbon.
But-2-ene plainly passes the test.
Each double-bonded carbon of but-2-ene carries H and CH3 - two different groups.

questions.stem: What relationship links the cis and trans forms of but-2-ene?

options.text: They are stereoisomers with the same molecular formula
options.explanation: Connectivity is identical; only the spatial arrangement differs.

options.text: They are different homologous series members
options.explanation: Both are C4H8 with the same backbone.

options.text: They are conformers interconverting at room temperature
options.explanation: Rotation is locked, so they cannot interconvert freely.
Isomers always share one formula.

questions.stem: State the two conditions needed for geometric isomerism about a C=C bond.
questions.modelAnswer: Rotation must be restricted by the double bond, and each alkene carbon must carry two different groups.

questions.stem: Define the terms cis and trans with respect to alkene geometry.
questions.modelAnswer: Cis describes the isomer whose matching groups share one side of the C=C; trans describes the isomer whose matching groups face each other across the C=C.

questions.stem: Explain why 2-methylpropene shows no geometric isomerism.
questions.modelAnswer: One alkene carbon carries two identical methyl groups, so swapping sides produces the same molecule - with only one possible arrangement, no geometric pair exists.

questions.stem: Draw and label the two geometric isomers of but-2-ene and give each name.
questions.modelAnswer: But-2-ene exists as cis-but-2-ene with both methyl groups parked on one side, and trans-but-2-ene with the methyl groups facing across the double bond.

questions.stem: Why does cis / trans naming break down for 2-methylpropene?

options.text: Its groups carry no hydrogens at all
options.explanation: Each methyl does carry hydrogens; the problem is the identical pair.

options.text: One alkene carbon carries two identical methyl groups
options.explanation: With no distinguishing pair, same-side versus opposite-side becomes meaningless.

options.text: The molecule contains no double bond
options.explanation: 2-methylpropene is plainly an alkene.
Chain length is irrelevant to naming rules.

questions.stem: Under CIP rules, which criterion sets substituent priority?

options.explanation: The rule is atomic number, not electronegativity.

options.text: Alphabetical order of the group name
options.explanation: Names are irrelevant to CIP ranking.

options.text: Atomic number of the directly bonded atom
options.explanation: Higher atomic number wins the higher priority.
Bulk plays no role; only atomic number counts.

questions.stem: An alkene parks its two highest-priority groups on one shared side. Its label is:

options.explanation: Entgegen - that label belongs to priorities facing across.
Cis only applies with hydrogens present on both carbons.
Trans has the same restriction as cis.
Zusammen - the top priorities park together on one side.

questions.stem: For 1-bromo-2-chloropropene, which atom wins the priority contest on its carbon?

options.explanation: 35 outranks every atom bonded alongside it.
17 beats carbon but not bromine on the same carbon's contest.
Carbon's 6 is the lowest here except hydrogen.
Hydrogen's 1 is always last in these contests.

questions.stem: Which compound can be named with cis / trans labels?

options.explanation: Substituted carbons without the required hydrogens need E / Z.
Each alkene carbon carries one H and one methyl group.
One carbon carries two methyls - cis / trans is undefined.
Neither alkene carbon carries a hydrogen.

questions.stem: State what the letters E and Z stand for and what each labels.
questions.modelAnswer: E is entgegen, the isomer whose two top-priority groups face each other across the C=C; Z is zusammen, the isomer whose two top-priority groups share one side.

questions.stem: Recall the CIP priority rule used in the E / Z system.
questions.modelAnswer: Substituents are ranked by the atomic number of the atom attached directly to the alkene carbon, the largest number taking the highest priority.

questions.stem: Explain why the E / Z system succeeds wherever cis / trans naming fails.
questions.modelAnswer: E / Z never mentions hydrogens - it ranks whatever groups are present by atomic number, so it still produces two distinct labels even when every substituent is carbon-based or halogen.

questions.stem: Assign E or Z to the isomer of 1-bromo-2-chloropropene in which Br and Cl sit on opposite sides, showing the priority working.
questions.modelAnswer: Priority on the first alkene carbon: Br (35) over H (1); on the second: Cl (17) over CH3 (6). With Br and Cl facing across the C=C, the two top priorities are separated, so the label is E.

questions.stem: A drawn alkene has its two highest-priority substituents on opposite sides. Name it:

options.explanation: Cis vocabulary does not apply to substituted pairs without hydrogens.
Trans labels need the one-H-each-carbon condition.
Entgegen - the priorities face across from each other.
Zusammen needs the priorities together.

questions.stem: In ranking CH2OH against CH3 on the same alkene carbon, which wins priority?

options.explanation: Frequency plays no part in CIP ranking.
The first point of difference breaks the tie immediately.
Size is irrelevant; atomic number decides.

options.text: CH2OH, because its carbon is bonded to oxygen
options.explanation: The oxygen (8) outranks the hydrogens (1) at the first point of difference.

questions.stem: What must you verify before assigning E or Z to any drawn alkene?

options.text: That each alkene carbon carries two different groups
options.explanation: Without that condition there is only one arrangement and no label to give.
Saturated molecules cannot show alkene stereochemistry at all.
The E / Z system never requires hydrogens.

options.text: That the drawing is to scale
options.explanation: Geometry is read from the drawing's arrangement, not its scale.

questions.stem: Two drawn structures differ only in which side one bromine-bearing group occupies. How should the pair be reported?

options.explanation: Both drawings carry the same molecular formula.

options.text: As two stereoisomers, one E and one Z
options.explanation: The pair differ in spatial arrangement only, so each gets its own label.
The drawings are different compounds - naming one loses the other.
Connectivity is identical, so they are stereo-, not structural, isomers.

questions.stem: Which atom's atomic number decides priority at the first point of difference on a functionalised alkene carbon?

options.text: The heaviest atom anywhere in the group
options.explanation: Only the first layer matters unless that layer ties.

options.text: The atom with the most bonds
options.explanation: Bond count is not the ranking key.

options.text: The atom directly bonded to the alkene carbon
options.explanation: First-layer atoms set the ranking before any deeper comparison.

options.text: The atom farthest along the chain
options.explanation: Comparison stops at the first difference; distance does not win.

questions.stem: State the two-line procedure for naming a drawn alkene in the E / Z system.
questions.modelAnswer: Rank the groups on each alkene carbon by atomic number of the attached atom, then label Z if the two winners share a side and E if they sit opposite.

questions.stem: Give the priority order of bromine, chlorine, the methyl group and hydrogen under CIP rules.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromine (35) ranks above chlorine (17), which ranks above the methyl carbon (6), which ranks above hydrogen (1).

questions.stem: Explain why 1-chloroprop-1-ene shows cis / trans isomerism while 1-bromo-2-chloropropene does not.
questions.modelAnswer: In 1-chloroprop-1-ene each alkene carbon still carries one hydrogen, so the cis / trans labels have a reference point; in 1-bromo-2-chloropropene both alkene carbons lack a hydrogen, so only the priority-based E / Z system applies.

questions.stem: A drawn pair shows 1-bromo-1-propen-2-ol with the OH-bearing carbon's hydrogen on opposite sides in the two drawings. Report each isomer's label.
questions.modelAnswer: Rank each carbon: Br (35) over CH2OH's carbon (6) on one side; CH2OH's oxygen-bearing carbon (6) over CH3 (6, broken by the O at the next layer). The drawing with the top priorities parked together is Z and the one with them facing apart is E.
